title: PMV Fundamentals
text:
Purpose of a PMV
The Passy-Muir Valve is a one-way speaking valve that allows:

Improved verbal communication
Restoration of upper airway airflow
Improved cough effectiveness
Improved secretion management
Potential improvements in swallowing
Improved quality of life

title: PMV Fundamentals
text:
PMV Prerequisites
Patients should generally demonstrate:
✔ Medical stability
✔ Awake and alert
✔ Deflated cuff
✔ Patent upper airway
✔ Ability to tolerate redirected airflow
✔ Manageable secretions
✔ Stable respiratory status

title: PMV Fundamentals

Inflated cuff

Unstable respiratory status
Significant air trapping
Severe secretion burden
Inability to tolerate cuff deflation

title: Clinical Decision
text:
Clinical Readiness Summary
Based on chart review, vital signs, and bedside presentation, Mr. Walker is not currently appropriate for a full clinical swallowing evaluation or PO trials.
Key factors include:

Acute large left MCA stroke
Reduced level of alertness
Inconsistent command following
Poor secretion management
Inability to participate in complete oral mechanism examination
Elevated blood pressure and ongoing medical monitoring


Clinical decision: Defer PO trials and continue NPO at this time.

Continue NPO

Which findings support proceeding with a PMV evaluation today?

A clinical swallow evaluation may include:

Review of medical history
Respiratory status
Mental status
Communication abilities
Oral mechanism examination
Secretion management
Voice and cough
Oral trials when appropriate
Clinical recommendations
Determination of whether instrumentation is indicated

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation

Instrumental assessment allows direct observation of swallowing anatomy, bolus flow, airway invasion, residue, and the effects of selected strategies.
The two primary instrumental assessments are:

Fiberoptic Endoscopic Evaluation of Swallowing
Modified Barium Swallow Study

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation
text:
Strengths

Available at bedside
Provides essential medical and functional context
Evaluates readiness and ability to participate
Allows assessment of oral motor function
Supports immediate clinical recommendations
Helps determine whether instrumentation is necessary

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation

A bedside evaluation cannot directly visualize:

Aspiration
Silent aspiration
Pharyngeal residue
Laryngeal penetration
Timing of airway invasion
Pharyngeal biomechanics


A patient may demonstrate aspiration without coughing or other obvious bedside signs.

Pharyngeal clearance

Swallowing biomechanics across lateral and anterior-posterior views

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation

Requires radiation exposure.

Represents a limited sample of swallowing performance.
Secretions are not directly visualized.
Vocal fold movement is not directly assessed.

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation
text:
Scenario 1
A patient in the ICU has copious secretions, a weak voice, and cannot safely leave the unit.


Reveal Discussion

FEES may be particularly useful.
It can be completed at bedside and allows direct assessment of secretions, laryngeal anatomy, airway protection, and pharyngeal residue.
A clinical swallow evaluation remains necessary for medical context and readiness.

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation
text:
Scenario 2
A patient following partial glossectomy demonstrates prolonged oral preparation and suspected reduced bolus propulsion.


Reveal Discussion

MBSS may be particularly useful when the primary question involves oral bolus preparation, oral transport, and bolus flow across swallowing phases.
FEES may also provide valuable information if secretion management, laryngeal function, or bedside assessment is the primary concern.
The correct selection depends on the clinical question.

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation
text:
Scenario 3
A patient with acute stroke has not yet received any swallowing assessment and is alert, medically stable, and able to participate.


Reveal Discussion

Begin with a clinical swallow evaluation unless the medical presentation or institutional pathway indicates immediate instrumentation.
Use the clinical assessment to identify risks, immediate recommendations, and unanswered questions.

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation
text:
Scenario 4
A patient demonstrates no coughing with liquids but has recurrent pneumonia and an unexplained oxygen requirement.


Reveal Discussion

The absence of coughing does not rule out aspiration.
Instrumentation should be considered because the bedside examination cannot reliably exclude silent aspiration.
FEES or MBSS may be appropriate depending on the specific clinical question, transport feasibility, and patient status.

title: Bedside Assessment and Instrumentation
text:
Scenario 5
A patient can tolerate only several minutes of transportation and positioning but requires repeated assessment of secretion management and airway protection.


Reveal Discussion

FEES may be preferred because it can be performed at bedside, directly visualizes secretions, and can be repeated without radiation exposure.

Instrumentation should answer a question that cannot be answered through bedside assessment alone.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text: Treatment should be selected based on the patient’s swallowing physiology, medical status, goals, cognition, endurance, and ability to participate.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
SLP Task
For each intervention, identify whether it is primarily compensatory, rehabilitative, or adjunctive. Be prepared to explain what impairment or clinical goal the intervention is intended to address.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Pneumonia
Swallowing treatment was associated with a reduced risk of pneumonia across the included studies.

The certainty of this evidence was rated as low, meaning the true effect may differ from the estimated effect.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Aspiration
The review did not find clear evidence that swallowing treatment reduced aspiration after treatment.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Return to Oral Intake
The review did not find clear evidence that treatment shortened the time required to return to oral intake.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Hospital Length of Stay
The review did not find clear evidence of a reduction in hospital length of stay.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Pharyngeal Residue
A small number of studies found improvement in pharyngeal residue severity, but the certainty of evidence was very low.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Overall Conclusion
The authors concluded that evidence supporting specific dysphagia interventions in acute and critical care remains limited.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Compensatory Strategies
Compensatory strategies are intended to improve swallowing safety or efficiency during use.
They do not necessarily create lasting physiologic change.
Examples may include:

Altering bolus volume
Altering rate of intake
Alternating solids and liquids
Upright positioning
Postural adjustments
Diet or liquid modification
Environmental modifications
Feeding assistance or supervision


A compensatory strategy should be selected because it addresses an identified clinical problem—not simply because it is commonly used.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Rehabilitative Interventions
Rehabilitative interventions are intended to produce longer-term changes in strength, coordination, range of motion, sensation, or swallowing physiology.
Interventions represented in the review included:

Tongue-palate resistance training
Respiratory muscle strength training
Chin tuck against resistance
Effortful swallowing exercises
Traditional swallowing exercises
Behavioral swallowing interventions

The review did not establish one exercise as universally effective for all acute care patients.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Sensory and Neurostimulation Interventions
The review also included:

Neuromuscular electrical stimulation
Pharyngeal electrical stimulation
Transcranial direct current stimulation
Transcranial magnetic stimulation
Acupuncture

Evidence varied considerably across interventions and outcomes. Several approaches remain specialized, emerging, or experimental within acute and critical care practice.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
1. Identify the Impairment
Examples:

Reduced lingual strength
Reduced bolus control
Reduced hyolaryngeal movement
Reduced pharyngeal clearance
Impaired airway closure
Reduced cough strength
Reduced endurance
Reduced sensation

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
2. Identify the Functional Consequence
Examples:

Anterior loss
Oral residue
Prolonged oral preparation
Pharyngeal residue
Penetration or aspiration
Inability to manage secretions
Inability to sustain a meal
Increased respiratory burden

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
3. Select an Intervention
Ask:

Does the intervention target the identified impairment?
Can the patient follow the directions?
Is the patient medically stable?
Can the patient complete the required intensity?
Is the treatment supported by instrumental findings?
Is the intervention appropriate for the current phase of recovery?
What outcome will be measured?

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
4. Reassess
Determine whether the intervention improves:

Swallow safety
Swallow efficiency
Oral intake
Secretion management
Patient comfort
Participation
Quality of life

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Scenario 1
A patient demonstrates reduced lingual strength and prolonged oral transit.
What intervention category might be appropriate?


Reveal Discussion

A rehabilitative intervention targeting lingual strength may be considered if the patient is medically stable and able to participate.
The specific exercise, intensity, and resistance should be individualized.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Scenario 2
A patient aspirates thin liquids during an instrumental assessment but demonstrates improved airway protection with a specific postural adjustment.
What intervention category is this?


Reveal Discussion

This is a compensatory strategy because it improves swallowing performance while the strategy is being used.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Scenario 3
A critically ill patient is significantly fatigued, inconsistently alert, and unable to follow multistep directions.
Would an intensive exercise program be appropriate today?


Reveal Discussion

Possibly not.
The treatment plan should reflect the patient’s medical stability, alertness, endurance, and capacity to participate. Initial management may instead prioritize positioning, oral care, secretion management, caregiver education, and reassessment.

title: Evidence-Based Dysphagia Treatment
text:
Evidence Pearl
Absence of strong evidence does not mean that all treatment is ineffective. It means clinicians should avoid overstating certainty, select interventions based on a defensible physiologic rationale, and measure patient-centered outcomes.

title: Simulation 4: AAC Consultation
text:
Simulation Overview
Patients in acute care may experience temporary or permanent barriers to communication related to neurological injury, intubation, motor impairment, sensory loss, language differences, pain, fatigue, or changes in cognition.
In this simulation, you will assume the role of the consulting speech-language pathologist. You will review several patient scenarios, identify barriers to functional communication, and recommend appropriate augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) supports.
Unlike previous simulations, this activity is primarily completed through the course website rather than through a mannequin-based encounter.

Clinical Focus
The goal of an acute care AAC consultation is not necessarily to identify the most advanced communication device. The immediate goal is to establish a reliable and efficient way for the patient to communicate medical needs, preferences, questions, and decisions.

title: Simulation 4: AAC Consultation
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this simulation, students will be able to:

Identify barriers affecting functional communication in the acute care setting.
Evaluate patient access abilities, including motor, visual, auditory, cognitive, and linguistic factors.
Select appropriate low-tech and high-tech AAC supports.
Develop strategies for communicating urgent medical and personal needs.
Provide patient, family, and staff education regarding AAC use.
Coordinate recommendations with the interdisciplinary team.
Document findings and recommendations using an acute care SOAP note.
Reflect on clinical reasoning and patient-centered decision-making.

title: Simulation 4: AAC Consultation
text:
Your Role
You are the speech-language pathologist responding to a communication consultation.
For each patient case, you will:

Review the reason for consultation.
Identify the primary communication barrier.
Evaluate available communication and access skills.
Select AAC strategies to trial.
Address the patient’s immediate communication needs.
Identify appropriate interdisciplinary follow-up.
Document your assessment and recommendations.

title: Simulation 4: AAC Consultation
text:
AAC Assessment Framework
When selecting an AAC approach, consider the following areas:







Area
Questions to Consider




Communication
Can the patient speak, vocalize, gesture, write, read, or answer yes/no questions?


Language
Does the patient understand spoken and written language? What is the patient’s preferred language?


Cognition
Can the patient attend, remember directions, make selections, and understand cause and effect?


Motor Access
Can the patient point, reach, lift a hand, move their head, or use eye gaze?


Vision
Can the patient see written words, pictures, colors, and communication targets?


Hearing
Can the patient hear conversational speech? Are hearing aids or amplification available?


Environment
Are noise, lighting, positioning, fatigue, or medical equipment affecting communication?


Urgency
What medical, safety, comfort, or personal needs must be communicated immediately?

Reveal Example Clinical Reasoning

The patient is alert, follows commands, and has severe motor limitations with no functional speech. Eye movement may represent the patient’s most reliable access method.
An initial low-tech system could include a large-print yes/no board and an eye-gaze communication board containing urgent messages such as pain, positioning, suction, bathroom, family, hot, cold, and call nurse.
Partner-assisted scanning could serve as a backup method. The communication partner would verbally present categories and choices while the patient uses the established yes/no response.
A high-tech eye-gaze speech-generating device could be considered if the communication impairment is expected to continue and the patient demonstrates adequate visual attention and language skills.
The most urgent concerns are pain, positioning, and hygiene. Nursing should be notified immediately, while the patient’s request to contact their partner should be addressed after consent is confirmed.

High-Tech AAC Options
High-tech AAC may include:

Tablet-based communication applications
Speech-generating devices
Eye-gaze speech-generating devices
Switch-access communication systems
Head-controlled devices
Text-to-speech applications
Personal voice amplifiers







Note



The most appropriate AAC method is the method the patient can use reliably, efficiently, and consistently. The most technologically advanced option is not always the best option.

title: AAC Consultation Resources
text:
Establishing Yes/No Responses
A reliable yes/no response is often the foundation of functional communication.

Possible Response Modes

Verbal response
Head nod or shake
Eye movement
Blink response
Thumb movement
Finger movement
Pointing to written choices
Switch activation



Reliability Check
Ask several questions with known answers.
Include:

Questions for which the answer is yes
Questions for which the answer is no
Questions related to personal information
Questions unrelated to immediate wants or needs

Avoid relying on a single response.

title: AAC Consultation Resources
text:
Partner-Assisted Scanning
Partner-assisted scanning may be useful when the patient cannot directly point to a communication target.
The communication partner:

Presents categories or choices.
Pauses after each option.
Watches for the patient’s established response.
Confirms the selected message.
Repeats the process as needed.

Example:

Are you uncomfortable because of pain, positioning, temperature, toileting, breathing, or something else?

title: AAC Consultation Resources
text:
Communication Partner Strategies
Staff and family should:

Gain the patient’s attention.
Face the patient.
Reduce distractions.
Use short, direct messages.
Ask one question at a time.
Allow adequate response time.
Verify yes/no responses.
Confirm the patient’s intended message.
Keep AAC materials within reach and view.
Document the established communication method.
Provide a backup communication strategy.

Interpreter Considerations
A qualified medical interpreter should be used for:

Medical assessment
Informed consent
Diagnosis and prognosis
Treatment education
Medical decision-making
Discharge planning
Complex symptom discussion

AAC may support immediate communication across languages but should not replace appropriate interpreter services.

title: AAC Consultation Resources
text:
Example Assessment Statement

Pt presents with impaired functional communication secondary to absent verbal output and severe motor limitations. Pt demonstrated reliable responses to concrete yes/no questions using upward eye gaze for yes and downward eye gaze for no. Pt successfully selected basic medical and comfort needs from a low-tech eye-gaze communication board with minimal cueing. Recommend continued use of established eye-gaze system with partner-assisted scanning available as a backup method.

title: AAC Consultation Resources
text:

Continue skilled ST intervention to establish an efficient and reliable AAC system for communication of basic wants, medical needs, and care preferences. Provide ongoing staff and family education and coordinate with OT and nursing regarding positioning, access, and bedside implementation.

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
1. Patient Preparation

Explain the procedure.
Confirm patient identity.
Review contraindications and precautions.
Position the patient.
Establish a method for communicating discomfort or requesting a pause.

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
2. Scope Passage

The scope is passed transnasally.
Nasal anatomy and patient tolerance are monitored.
The scope is advanced to obtain a view of the pharynx and larynx.

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
3. Anatomic and Functional Examination
The clinician may observe:

Base of tongue
Valleculae
Epiglottis
Arytenoids
False vocal folds
True vocal folds
Pyriform sinuses
Posterior pharyngeal wall
Secretion location
Spontaneous swallowing
Vocal fold movement
Cough or throat-clear response

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
4. Swallowing Trials
Trials are selected based on the clinical question and patient status.
The clinician may assess:

Premature spillage
Penetration
Aspiration before or after the swallow
Residue location and severity
Secretion management
Response to bolus modification
Response to posture or strategy
Fatigue across trials

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Before the Swallow

Secretions
Premature spillage
Material entering the laryngeal vestibule before the swallow
Baseline airway status

title: FEES Demonstration
text:

Pharyngeal residue
Laryngeal penetration
Aspiration below the vocal folds
Patient response to airway invasion
Effectiveness of clearing swallows or strategies

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Anatomy

Are the structures symmetrical?
Is there edema?
Is there evidence of trauma or lesion?
Do the vocal folds abduct and adduct?

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Secretions

Are secretions present?
Where are they located?
Does the patient respond?
Can the patient clear them?

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Airway Protection

Is penetration present?
Is aspiration present?
Does the patient cough?
Is the response effective?
Is airway invasion cleared?

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Efficiency

Is residue present?
Where is residue located?
Does it increase across trials?
Does an additional swallow reduce residue?

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Strategy Testing

Does a postural adjustment improve performance?
Does changing volume or consistency improve performance?
Can the patient implement the strategy independently?

title: FEES Demonstration
text:
Clinical Pearl
FEES is not simply a test for aspiration. It provides information about anatomy, secretions, sensation, airway protection, residue, fatigue, and response to intervention.

text: A focused oral mechanism examination helps the SLP describe the integrity and function of structures involved in speech and swallowing.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text: A focused oral mechanism examination helps the SLP describe the integrity and function of structures involved in speech and swallowing.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
SLP Task
Work with a partner. One person performs the examination while the other identifies the cranial nerve, expected response, and possible functional implications.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Before You Begin
A cranial nerve examination is only one component of the clinical assessment.
An isolated abnormal finding does not independently diagnose dysphagia or aspiration. Interpret findings alongside the patient’s medical history, respiratory status, cognition, communication abilities, secretion management, and swallowing presentation.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
section: Cranial Nerves Relevant to Speech and Swallowing
text:
Cranial Nerves Relevant to Speech and Swallowing









Cranial Nerve
Primary Functions
Focused Assessment
Possible Functional Relevance




CN V: Trigeminal
Jaw movement; facial and oral sensation
Open and close jaw; clench teeth; assess jaw strength and symmetry; assess facial sensation when indicated
Mastication, oral preparation, awareness of material in the oral cavity


CN VII: Facial
Facial movement; lip closure; taste to anterior tongue
Smile; pucker; retract lips; puff cheeks; assess facial symmetry
Labial seal, anterior containment, oral pressure


CN IX: Glossopharyngeal
Pharyngeal sensation; taste to posterior tongue; contribution to pharyngeal movement
Consider sensory response and patient report; gag testing is not routinely necessary
Pharyngeal sensation and sensory input for swallowing


CN X: Vagus
Palatal movement; phonation; laryngeal function; cough; pharyngeal movement
Observe palate during sustained “ah”; assess voice quality; voluntary cough; secretion management
Airway protection, vocal fold function, pharyngeal movement


CN XI: Spinal Accessory
Head turn and shoulder elevation
Shoulder shrug; turn head against resistance
Positioning and ability to use some postural strategies


CN XII: Hypoglossal
Tongue movement
Protrude tongue; lateralize; elevate; depress; assess strength and symmetry
Bolus formation, manipulation, propulsion, oral clearance

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Question 1
A patient presents with reduced lip closure and anterior loss of liquids.


Reveal Answer

CN VII: Facial
CN VII contributes to facial movement and labial closure. Reduced function may affect anterior containment and generation of oral pressure.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Question 2
A patient demonstrates reduced tongue lateralization and difficulty clearing food from the lateral sulci.


Reveal Answer

CN XII: Hypoglossal
CN XII supports tongue movement for bolus manipulation, lateralization, propulsion, and oral clearance.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Question 3
A patient presents with a breathy voice and weak voluntary cough.


Reveal Answer

CN X: Vagus
These findings may raise concern for impaired laryngeal function or airway protection. They do not independently confirm aspiration.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Question 4
A patient demonstrates reduced jaw opening and weak mastication.


Reveal Answer

CN V: Trigeminal
CN V supports jaw movement and contributes to oral sensation.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Question 5
A patient is unable to maintain an upright head position or turn the head adequately.


Reveal Answer

CN XI: Spinal Accessory
CN XI supports shoulder elevation and head turning. Weakness may affect positioning and the feasibility of some compensatory postures.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Face and Lips

Observe facial symmetry at rest.
Ask the patient to smile.
Ask the patient to pucker.
Ask the patient to puff the cheeks.
Assess lip strength and ability to maintain pressure.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Jaw

Observe jaw position at rest.
Ask the patient to open and close the jaw.
Assess lateral jaw movement.
Assess strength when clinically appropriate.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Tongue

Observe the tongue at rest.
Ask the patient to protrude the tongue.
Ask the patient to move the tongue left and right.
Ask the patient to elevate and depress the tongue.
Assess strength against resistance when appropriate.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Palate and Voice

Ask the patient to sustain “ah.”
Observe palatal movement and symmetry.
Listen to vocal quality.
Assess loudness and phonatory stability.
Ask for a voluntary cough or throat clear when appropriate.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Secretion Management

Observe the patient’s ability to manage saliva.
Note drooling, frequent suctioning, wet vocal quality, or visible secretions.
Consider alertness, respiratory status, and spontaneous swallowing frequency.

title: Cranial Nerves and Oral Mechanism Examination
text:
Clinical Pearl
Do not interpret the gag reflex as a stand-alone measure of swallowing safety. The Bours systematic review found that single clinical features, including an abnormal gag or volitional cough, generally demonstrated limited diagnostic usefulness when used alone.

title: Functional Implications
text:
Connecting Cognitive Domains to Function
After completing the MoCA during simulation, use the results to describe how cognitive-communication deficits may affect Cindy’s daily functioning and discharge needs.

title: Functional Implications
text:
Domain-to-Function Guide







Cognitive Domain
Possible Functional Implications




Attention
Difficulty sustaining focus during therapy, meals, safety routines, and conversations


Visuospatial / Executive Function
Difficulty scanning the environment, completing multi-step tasks, navigating safely, and recognizing hazards


Memory
Difficulty recalling recent events, new safety instructions, medication changes, and therapy recommendations


Orientation
Confusion regarding place, date, situation, and hospital routines


Language
Word errors or communication breakdowns that may affect medical communication


Insight / Awareness
Reduced recognition of deficits, increased fall risk, and difficulty following safety precautions

title: Functional Implications
text:
Right Hemisphere Stroke Considerations

Right hemisphere stroke may affect attention, awareness, visual scanning, pragmatics, safety judgment, and functional problem-solving. A screening score alone does not fully describe functional impact.

title: Functional Implications
text:
Clinical Impression Prompts
Use your MoCA results and chart review to answer:

Which cognitive domains appear most impacted?
How do these deficits affect safety and participation in rehabilitation?
What recommendations would support Cindy and her spouse?
What additional assessment or follow-up may be needed?

title: Functional Implications
text:
Possible Recommendations
Recommendations may include:

Continue SLP cognitive-communication intervention
Provide family education regarding cognitive changes after right hemisphere stroke
Use environmental supports for left attention/scanning
Provide written and verbal reminders for safety information
Coordinate with OT/PT regarding neglect, mobility, and safety concerns
Consider supervision needs at discharge based on functional performance


Clinical takeaway: The goal is not only to report a score, but to explain what the findings mean for Cindy’s safety, participation, and everyday life.

title: Simulation 7
text:
SLP Task
Work through each module with your group. Review the patient’s medical history and interdisciplinary documentation, determine readiness for PMV evaluation, complete a PMV and clinical swallowing evaluation, and develop recommendations regarding communication, oral intake, and need for further assessment.

title: Simulation 7
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, students will be able to:

Integrate medical and interdisciplinary information relevant to PMV and swallowing evaluation.
Determine readiness for Passy-Muir Valve assessment in a medically complex patient.
Conduct a focused clinical swallowing evaluation in the acute care setting.
Identify clinical findings associated with increased risk for oropharyngeal dysphagia.
Interpret bedside findings within the context of respiratory, medical, and nutritional status.
Identify the limitations of the clinical swallowing evaluation.
Determine when instrumental swallowing assessment is indicated.
Develop appropriate recommendations for communication, oral intake, and continued dysphagia management.
Document clinical findings and recommendations using professional medical terminology.

title: PMV & Swallowing Considerations
text: Karla has been referred for both Passy-Muir Valve assessment and swallowing evaluation. Before entering the room, determine how you will approach today’s evaluation and what information you need to obtain.

title: PMV & Swallowing Considerations
text:
SLP Task
Use information from the chart and interdisciplinary documentation to plan your evaluation. Be prepared to explain the order of your assessment, identify safety considerations, and justify when you would proceed, modify, or discontinue the evaluation.

title: PMV & Swallowing Considerations
text:
Before Entering the Room
Discuss the following with your group:

What information should be confirmed before beginning a PMV trial?
What equipment or supplies should be available during the evaluation?
Which baseline measures should be obtained before cuff deflation or PMV placement?
What signs would suggest that Karla is tolerating cuff deflation?
What findings would make you delay or discontinue PMV placement?
How might Karla’s current respiratory status influence the duration of the evaluation?

title: PMV & Swallowing Considerations
text:
PMV and Swallowing
Consider how PMV use may relate to the swallowing portion of today’s evaluation.

Discuss:

If Karla tolerates PMV placement, would you complete the clinical swallowing evaluation with the valve in place? Why or why not?
Does successful PMV tolerance indicate that swallowing is safe?
How might restoring airflow through the upper airway affect your ability to evaluate:

Vocal quality
Cough strength
Secretion management
Patient communication

What information obtained during the PMV trial may also be relevant to the swallowing evaluation?

title: PMV & Swallowing Considerations
text:
Planning the Clinical Swallowing Evaluation
Karla has several factors that may influence today’s bedside assessment.
Consider:

Recent prolonged intubation
Tracheostomy placement
Acute respiratory illness
Reduced endurance
Mild cognitive impairment
Pre-hospital coughing during meals
Reduced oral intake
Unintentional weight loss


Discuss:

What components should be included in a focused oral mechanism examination?
What aspects of Karla’s respiratory status should be monitored during PO trials?
Which consistencies would you consider presenting during the evaluation?
How will you determine whether to continue, modify, or discontinue PO trials?
What findings can be identified during a clinical swallowing evaluation?
What important information cannot be determined from bedside assessment alone?

title: PMV & Swallowing Considerations
text:
Clinical Reminder
The purpose of the clinical swallowing evaluation is not to determine whether aspiration is definitively present or absent.
Use the bedside assessment to characterize swallowing function, identify clinical signs and risk factors, determine immediate safety considerations, and decide whether additional assessment is warranted.
